analogy.p: A cell is like a huge factory: assembly lines (enzymes) turn raw materials (glucose, nitrate, fatty acids) into products (starch, lipids, proteins), while a recycling unit converts waste (excess amino acids) into a disposal product (urea). Respiration is the power station that supplies the electricity (energy) to all lines. Everything happening in the whole factory at once is metabolism. The analogy breaks down because a factory is run by managers, whereas cells are controlled by enzymes and chemical feedback with no central decision-maker.
analogy.t: A factory with a power station

bullets: Definition: **metabolism = the sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body**.
The reactions are **enzyme controlled** and continual (they never stop while the organism is alive).
They are driven by **energy transferred by respiration**.
Know **five examples** and the raw materials/products of each.
Links closely to enzymes (4.2), respiration (4.4.1) and homeostasis (4.5).
Exam marks are usually 1 to 4: define, list examples, or describe one reaction.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 4.4.3 'Metabolism' asks you to know that **metabolism is the sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body**, that the energy from respiration drives these **continual enzyme-controlled processes**, and to recall five named examples. These examples are the conversion of glucose to starch, glycogen and cellulose; the formation of lipids from glycerol and fatty acids; the use of glucose and nitrate ions to make amino acids and then proteins; respiration; and the breakdown of excess protein to form urea. It is a short section but the examples are easy marks if learned exactly.

bullets: Metabolism includes **all** reactions in a cell, not just respiration.
Reactions that **build up** molecules need energy; reactions that **break down** molecules often release energy.
Each metabolic reaction is catalysed by a specific **enzyme**.
Metabolism happens in both **cells** and the **whole body** (e.g. liver reactions).
Metabolic rate rises when you exercise because more respiration occurs.
Mark scheme wording: **'the sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body'**.
core.h: Metabolism: the sum of all reactions
core.p: Inside every living cell thousands of chemical reactions occur at the same time. Some build large molecules from small ones, while others break large molecules down to release energy or to get rid of waste. Together they are called metabolism. Because they happen at body temperature, they need **enzymes** to speed them up, and they need a constant supply of energy.

bullets: **Enzymes** are proteins that act as biological catalysts.
They work best at an **optimum temperature and pH**; extremes **denature** them.
Respiration releases energy from glucose; this is used for **building molecules**, **movement** and **active transport**.
Metabolic reactions are therefore described as **'enzyme-controlled processes'**.
Without enough energy, synthesis reactions (e.g. making proteins) slow down.
Link: respiration is itself part of metabolism, so metabolism is partly self-supplying.
core.h: Why enzymes and energy are needed
core.p: Enzymes are biological **catalysts**, which means they speed up reactions without being used up. Each enzyme has an **active site** with a shape that matches only its own substrate (the lock and key idea), so each metabolic reaction needs its own enzyme. Many reactions that build molecules need an input of energy, and this energy comes from **respiration**. If respiration stopped, metabolism would stop and the organism would die.

bullets: **Glucose → starch**: storage carbohydrate in plants (e.g. in roots, seeds, chloroplasts).
**Glucose → cellulose**: forms strong **cell walls** in plant cells that support the plant.
**Glucose → glycogen**: stored in the **liver and muscle** in animals.
Starch and glycogen are insoluble, so they do not affect the water balance of cells.
Glycogen can be broken back to glucose when blood glucose is low (link to glucagon).
These are all built from **many glucose molecules joined together**.
Starch is tested for with **iodine solution** (turns blue-black).
core.h: Converting glucose to starch, glycogen and cellulose
core.p: Glucose is a simple sugar. Many glucose molecules can be joined together in long chains to make larger carbohydrates. In plants, glucose is converted to **starch** (for storage) and **cellulose** (to make cell walls). In animals (and some other organisms) glucose is converted to **glycogen**, a storage carbohydrate found in the liver and muscles.

bullets: Exact recall: **1 glycerol + 3 fatty acids → 1 lipid molecule**.
Reverse reaction: during digestion, **lipase** breaks lipids into **glycerol and fatty acids**.
Lipids store **more energy per gram** than carbohydrates.
Lipids form part of **cell membranes** and insulate the body.
Fatty acids and glycerol absorbed after digestion are re-assembled into lipids in the body.
Lipids can be tested for with **ethanol** (cloudy emulsion) or Sudan III.
core.h: Forming lipids from glycerol and fatty acids
core.p: Lipids (fats and oils) are made from smaller building blocks. **One molecule of glycerol joins with three molecules of fatty acids** to make one lipid molecule. This is a metabolic reaction that is controlled by enzymes. Lipids are used as an energy store, for insulation and in **cell membranes**.

bullets: **Glucose + nitrate ions → amino acids** (the spec wording).
Nitrate ions supply the **nitrogen** (N) needed for amino acids.
**Amino acids → proteins**: joined in a specific order to make enzymes, hormones, antibodies and structural proteins.
Proteins are essential for growth and repair of tissue.
Plants lacking nitrate show **stunted growth** and **yellow leaves**.
Amino acids contain an amine group (NH2) and a carboxyl group; the order decides the protein's shape and function.
Proteins are tested for with **Biuret reagent** (blue to purple).
core.p: Plants make amino acids by combining **glucose** with **nitrate ions** absorbed from the soil. Nitrate provides the **nitrogen** needed, since glucose contains only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. These amino acids are then joined in long chains to **synthesise proteins**. Animals mostly get amino acids from digesting the protein in their food.

bullets: Aerobic: **glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water**.
Anaerobic (muscles): **glucose → lactic acid**.
Respiration happens continuously in all living cells.
The energy transferred is used for **building larger molecules** from smaller ones.
Also used for **muscle contraction** and **keeping warm** in mammals and birds.
Respiration is an example of a reaction that **breaks down** a molecule.
core.p: Respiration is itself a metabolic reaction. It is an **exothermic** reaction in which glucose is broken down to transfer energy. This energy is then used for all the other metabolic reactions as well as movement, keeping warm and active transport. Respiration is therefore the 'energy supplier' of metabolism.

bullets: Excess amino acids are broken down in the **liver** (deamination).
The product is **urea**, a toxic waste that must be removed.
Urea is carried in the **blood plasma** to the kidneys.
The **kidneys** remove urea in the **urine**.
Some urea is also lost in **sweat**.
**Excretion** = removal of metabolic waste products from the body.
Kidney failure causes a build-up of urea in the blood.
core.h: Breakdown of excess proteins to form urea
core.p: Proteins cannot be stored in the body, so any amino acids not needed are broken down in the **liver**. The nitrogen-containing part is converted into **urea**, which is a waste product. Urea is transported in the blood to the **kidneys**, which filter it out and it leaves the body in **urine**. This is called excretion.

bullets: **Photosynthesis** makes the glucose that plants then use in metabolism.
**Digestion** supplies glucose, amino acids, glycerol and fatty acids in animals.
**Liver**: glycogen storage, urea production, lactic acid to glucose conversion.
**Ribosomes** build proteins from amino acids.
Metabolism supports **growth, repair and energy transfer**.
Hormones such as insulin and glucagon control glucose metabolism.
core.h: Where reactions happen and how they link
core.p: Metabolic reactions occur in many places. Building reactions occur in the **cytoplasm** and on **ribosomes** (proteins), respiration occurs mostly in **mitochondria**, and photosynthesis in **chloroplasts** also feeds metabolism with glucose. The liver is the key organ for metabolism in humans because it stores glycogen, makes urea and processes lactic acid.

bullets: **Building up**: glucose → starch/glycogen/cellulose; glycerol + fatty acids → lipid; glucose + nitrate → amino acids → proteins.
**Breaking down**: respiration; excess protein → urea.
Building reactions use energy from respiration.
Breaking down in digestion also supplies small molecules to build with.
Do not forget digestion examples may be asked in a metabolism context.
The words 'anabolic' and 'catabolic' are often used at A level but are not needed for GCSE.
core.h: Building up and breaking down: organising your revision
core.p: A helpful way to organise the five examples is to sort them into reactions that **build** larger molecules from smaller ones and reactions that **break down** molecules. Building reactions need energy; breaking down reactions can release it. This is an extra way of thinking; the exam only needs the spec examples.

bullets: Define: **'sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body'**.
For examples give **both reactants and products**.
If asked 'why is energy needed?': for building up larger molecules and other metabolic processes.
Rate graphs: reaction rate rises with temperature to the optimum and then falls (enzyme denatured).
Be precise: **three** fatty acids and **one** glycerol.
Use the word **'nitrate ions'**, not 'nitrates in fertiliser' only.
core.p: Metabolism questions at GCSE are generally short. Learn the five examples as word equations. Questions on enzymes, temperature and rate of reaction may be combined with metabolism because all metabolic reactions are enzyme controlled.

bullets: **Enzymes (4.2)**: all reactions need specific enzymes with complementary active sites.
**Homeostasis (4.5)**: insulin converts glucose to glycogen; glucagon reverses it.
**Photosynthesis (4.4.1)**: produces glucose which enters plant metabolism.
**Kidneys (4.5)**: remove urea made in the liver.
Higher: explain why fever above about 40°C is dangerous: enzymes denature and metabolism fails.
Higher: explain that a lack of nitrate ions limits protein synthesis and so plant growth.
core.h: Links to other topics and Higher tier extension
core.p: Higher tier questions may ask you to link metabolism to enzyme function, homeostasis or the effect of disease. For example, explaining why a high body temperature can disrupt metabolism ties together enzyme denaturation and the loss of enzyme-controlled reactions.

exam: **Define metabolism** (1 mark): 'the sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body'.
**Give/state** (1 to 2 marks): learn the five examples exactly as in the specification.
**Describe** (2 marks): give reactants and product, e.g. 'one glycerol and three fatty acids join to form a lipid'.
**Explain** (2 to 3 marks): link to energy, nitrogen or enzyme function using 'because'.
Say **'nitrate ions'** when linking to amino acids and **'urea'** for excretion.
For 'where is urea made / removed': made in the **liver**, removed by **kidneys** in **urine**.
Do not confuse starch (plants) with glycogen (animals).
6 mark structure: define metabolism, then describe building reactions, respiration, protein breakdown, with enzymes and energy links.
If asked about enzymes in metabolism mention **active site, specific shape, optimum temperature and pH, denature**.
Use correct spelling of key terms: glycerol, glycogen, cellulose, lipid, urea.

mistakes.r: Metabolism is the sum of ALL reactions in a cell or the body; respiration is just one of them.
mistakes.w: Metabolism is another word for respiration.

mistakes.r: One glycerol molecule joins with three fatty acids.
mistakes.w: A lipid is made from glycerol and one fatty acid.

mistakes.r: They need glucose and nitrate ions (the source of nitrogen).
mistakes.w: Plants make amino acids from glucose only.

mistakes.r: Urea is made in the liver and removed by the kidneys.
mistakes.w: Urea is made in the kidneys.

mistakes.r: Starch is the plant store; glycogen is the animal store.
mistakes.w: Glycogen is the plant storage carbohydrate.

mistakes.r: Proteins are not stored; excess amino acids are broken down to urea.
mistakes.w: Excess protein is stored for later.

mistakes.r: They are enzyme controlled and use energy from respiration.

summary: AQA 4.4.3 asks you to know that metabolism is the sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body, driven by energy from respiration and controlled by enzymes, with five named examples: glucose to starch, glycogen and cellulose; lipid formation; amino acid and protein synthesis; respiration; and urea formation from excess protein. It matters because these examples link nutrition, enzymes and excretion.

terms.d: The sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body.
A biological catalyst that speeds up a specific reaction without being used up.
A simple sugar made in photosynthesis and used in respiration; a starting material for many metabolic reactions.
A storage carbohydrate in plants made from many glucose molecules.
A storage carbohydrate in animals, made from glucose and stored in the liver and muscles.
A carbohydrate made from glucose that forms plant cell walls.
A fat or oil made from one molecule of glycerol and three molecules of fatty acids.
A small molecule that joins with three fatty acids to form a lipid.
A building block of lipids; three join to one glycerol molecule.
A small molecule that is a building block of proteins.
A large molecule made of many amino acids; includes enzymes, antibodies and hormones.
Ions absorbed by plant roots that provide nitrogen for making amino acids.
A waste substance made in the liver from the breakdown of excess amino acids.
The removal of waste products of metabolism from the body.
An exothermic reaction in cells that transfers energy from glucose.

worked.ans: Metabolism is the sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body. Examples include conversion of glucose to glycogen and the formation of lipids from glycerol and three fatty acids.
worked.q: What is meant by metabolism? Give two examples. (3 marks)
steps: Definition: the sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body.
Example 1: glucose is converted to starch / glycogen / cellulose.
Example 2: a glycerol molecule joins with three fatty acids to make a lipid.

worked.ans: Plants use nitrate ions together with glucose to make amino acids, which are then used to synthesise proteins needed for growth. Without nitrate, protein synthesis is limited and growth is stunted.
worked.q: Explain why plants need nitrate ions. (3 marks)
steps: They combine with glucose to make amino acids.
Amino acids are joined to make proteins needed for growth.

worked.ans: Excess amino acids are broken down in the liver to form urea. The urea is carried in the blood to the kidneys, where it is removed and excreted in the urine.
worked.q: Describe what happens to excess amino acids in the human body. (3 marks)
steps: Urea in blood to kidneys and excreted in urine.
